# Vendored crates

Each directory is a copy of a published crate with local fixes, used through
`[patch.crates-io]` in the workspace `Cargo.toml`. They are temporary: when
upstream publishes a release with the fix, switch back to it and delete the
copy. Check the conditions below when updating dependencies.

| Crate | Base | Why | Switch back when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gpui` | 0.2.2 | **Not built by the application since the GPUI migration (#1081).** The application uses `gpui-pre` 0.3.12 (the rows below); this 0.2.2 copy stays as the reference the patches were re-applied from and for its Linux clipboard unit test in CI. Delete it once nothing needs that reference. Windows IME keys, Linux decorations, atlas reuse and more; see `gpui/PATCHES.md` | A GPUI release contains every fix in `gpui/PATCHES.md`, including running quit handlers on Windows `WM_ENDSESSION` (or they are no longer needed) |
| `gpui-pre` | 0.3.12 | The `queue` and Wayland `layer_shell` modules are also compiled on `freebsd` (#1081); `InputHandler::prefers_direct_input` (direct-input fields detach the IME), `App::on_quit_request`, `Menu::menu_type` phrase-aware wrapping (`StyledText::with_wrap_joins`) and hoverable link tooltips (`InteractiveText::hoverable_tooltip`). See `gpui-pre/PATCHES.md`. The other patches are re-applied later (`spec/gpui-kit-migration-2026-11-18.md`) | A `gpui-pre` release builds on FreeBSD and has `prefers_direct_input`, `on_quit_request` and `Menu::menu_type` |
| `gpui-pre-windows`, `gpui-pre-macos`, `gpui-pre-linux` | 0.3.12 | Direct-input fields (#1081): Windows drops the commit that ends the composition when the IME is detached, macOS limits the input sources to Roman, Wayland asks `query_ime_enabled`; macOS `applicationShouldTerminate:` and the Window menu type; Windows `IsWindow` before teardown and no simulated Alt when our own window is in front; clipboard limits (32 MiB pipe reads and a cancellable background Wayland read with a 5 second deadline, 16 MiB Windows text). See each `PATCHES.md` | A release has `prefers_direct_input` |
| `rav1d` | 1.1.0 | A damaged AV1 stream can reach an `unwrap` in an error path of `dav1d_send_data` (`extern "C"`, cannot unwind), which aborts the process; AVIF previews decode untrusted files with it (D018). Without the unused assembly; see `rav1d/PATCHES.md` | A `rav1d` release no longer aborts on the data of `crates/media/tests/avif_mutations.rs` (run it with a large `AVIF_MUTATIONS`) |
| `zed-xim` | 0.4.0-zed | Lenient COMPOUND_TEXT decoding instead of panics (IBus/Mozc), XIM input style selection, bounded data property atoms | A `zed-xim` release decodes COMPOUND_TEXT without panicking and bounds the atoms; the style selection would move back into GPUI |
| `irc-proto` | 1.1.0 | `LineCodec` rejects lines over 16 KiB (`MAX_LINE_BYTES`); upstream buffers a line without limit. Its `encoding` feature uses `encoding_rs` instead of the unmaintained `encoding` crate (RUSTSEC-2021-0153), and the workspace enables it directly rather than through `irc`'s `encoding` feature. `charsets` lets the codec convert the text of a `PRIVMSG`/`NOTICE` to a given target with another encoding than the rest of the line (per-channel `/charset`, #396). `LineCodec::encode` drops a line holding CR, LF or NUL besides the final `\r\n`, so no line, including the `irc` crate's own PONG and CTCP replies, can inject a command (#554). `line::is_single_line` is public so irc-core's transcript uses the same check (#573) | An `irc-proto` release limits the line length in its codec and decodes legacy charsets with a maintained crate; `irc`'s `encoding` feature must then no longer pull in `encoding` |
| `irc` | 1.1.0 | A received KICK of our own nickname drops the channel's `channel-lists` entry, like a PART we send does (`src/client/mod.rs`). "Our own nickname" is the one the server confirmed (RPL_WELCOME, then our own NICK), not `current_nickname()`, which ignores later nick changes. `Client::forget_channel_list` lets irc-core drop the list when its own casemapping-aware check sees the KICK, because the built-in check is ASCII-only (`nick{1}` vs `nick[1]`). Upstream only removed the kicked user, so a rejoin appended to stale entries: modes went to the old entry, members who left meanwhile stayed, and `list_channels()` still reported the channel (#342). A list exists only for a channel we joined: our own JOIN creates it empty (dropping an old one) and a NAMES reply for any other channel is ignored (upstream tracked it without limit). The first NAMES line after an end of NAMES (366) rebuilds the list and a nickname is listed once, so PART, QUIT and MODE reach it after a repeated NAMES (#597). Only the first end of MOTD (376/422) of a connection joins the configured channels; later ones join nothing, and the JOIN of every tracked channel is gone (#597). Member lists are bounded (50,000 members and 16 MiB per channel; 100,000 members, 32 MiB and 2,000 channels per connection; a NICK that lengthens an entry counts too; an entry counts its strings and 128 bytes, kept in a ledger updated by each list change; a refreshed or shrunk list gives back its capacity and a `User` keeps each access level once): NAMES, JOIN or NICK over a limit returns the new `Error::ChannelListLimit`, which ends the connection (#677). The `body-charsets` feature adds `Config::body_charsets`, handed to the line codec for per-channel text encodings (#396) The outgoing queue (`src/client/queue.rs`) holds at most 1024 messages and 1 MiB; upstream's was unbounded, so a server that sent `PING` faster than the socket drained piled up automatic `PONG`s. Every send, automatic replies included, passes the limit, and a full queue fails with `Error::OutgoingQueueFull` (`QUIT` alone is always admitted so it is written behind a backlog), which ends the connection like any stream error (#678). The clock reads (the keepalive `PING` data, the CTCP `PING` and the `TIME` reply) use `jiff` instead of the unmaintained `chrono` (RUSTSEC-2026-0543, #1068) | `Client` is no longer used (#266); upstream 1.1.0 is the latest release and has no fix |

`irc` and `rav1d` set `[lints.rust] warnings = "allow"` in their
`Cargo.toml`: their upstream code has unused items and old idioms that Cargo
would hide in a crates.io dependency, and fixing them here would only widen
the difference from upstream. Keep local fixes warning-free all the same.

Run the copies' own tests with `cargo test -p zed-xim` and
`cargo test -p irc-proto` (CI does both on Linux).

The `irc` copy is not a workspace member (its examples and dev-dependencies
are not vendored), so `cargo test -p irc` does not run here. To run its unit
tests, copy `vendor/irc` and `vendor/irc-proto` into a scratch directory, drop
the `[[example]]` tables, add an empty `[workspace]` and a `[patch.crates-io]`
entry for `irc-proto`, then run
`cargo test --no-default-features --features channel-lists,ctcp,tls-rust`.
